name: OSI, TCP/IP, TCP and UDP
author: Recurse
subject: networking
description: Place protocols on OSI and TCP/IP layers, trace encapsulation, and compare TCP and UDP behavior and well-known ports.

resources.title: Jeremy's IT Lab: TCP and UDP (Day 30)
resources.note: Free CCNA lecture: headers, handshake, windowing and port numbers.

resources.title: Jeremy's IT Lab: OSI Model and TCP/IP Suite (Day 3)
resources.note: Free CCNA lecture on layers, encapsulation and PDUs.

resources.title: RFC 9293: Transmission Control Protocol
resources.note: The current TCP standard; skim the header and state diagrams.

resources.title: RFC 768: User Datagram Protocol
resources.note: All of UDP in three pages, which says a lot.

resources.title: IANA Service Name and Port Number Registry

lesson.intro: Engineers talk in layers: a Layer 2 problem, a Layer 4 port. This pack builds the OSI and TCP/IP map, follows data as it is wrapped and unwrapped, then goes deep on TCP and UDP and the ports the CCNA expects you to know on sight.
objectives: Place protocols, devices and PDUs on OSI and TCP/IP layers
Trace encapsulation and say which headers change at each router
Map each TCP feature to its header field, and say what UDP leaves out
Work through handshakes, acknowledgments and windows with real numbers
Choose TCP or UDP for an application and recall its port

sections.title: The OSI model: a map for finding problems
sections.key: OSI splits networking into seven layers, each with one job; its layer numbers are the shared vocabulary and a bottom-up troubleshooting checklist.
sections.body:
A user says the internet is broken. A good engineer does not guess: cable and link lights first, then whether the switch port is up/up, then the PC's IP address, mask and gateway, then whether the port is reachable, then the application. That walk from wires to software is the **OSI reference model** at work.

[[visual]]

Real networks run TCP/IP protocols, but everyone uses OSI numbers: Layer 1 means cabling and signals, Layer 3 IP and routing, Layer 4 ports.

[[visual 2]]

Layers let each piece change alone: Wi-Fi replaces Ethernet and the browser never notices. Mnemonic from Layer 1 up: **P**lease **D**o **N**ot **T**hrow **S**ausage **P**izza **A**way.

layers.label: Application
layers.detail: network services for apps: HTTP, DNS, SMTP, SSH, DHCP

layers.label: Presentation
layers.detail: formats, encoding, encryption: ASCII, JPEG, MPEG

layers.label: Transport
layers.detail: right app, reliability, flow control: TCP, UDP, ports

layers.label: Network
layers.detail: logical addressing, routing: IPv4, IPv6, ICMP, routers

layers.label: Data link
layers.detail: delivery on one link: MAC, FCS, Ethernet, 802.11, switches

layers.label: Physical
layers.detail: bits as signals: cables, connectors, hubs, radio

items.title: Adjacent-layer interaction
points: Each layer serves the layer above
IP delivers packets so TCP can deliver bytes to apps

items.title: Same-layer interaction
points: A layer talks to its peer through the header it adds
The sender's TCP writes a sequence number; the receiver's TCP reads it

sections.tip: Troubleshoot bottom up when you have no clues: cable and link (1), interface up/up and MACs (2), IP, mask and gateway (3), ports and filters (4), then the app (7).
sections.pitfall: Placing encryption or data formats at Layer 7 because apps do it. In OSI, formats, encoding and encryption are Layer 6, Presentation; Layer 7 is the network service the app uses.

activity.title: Sort it onto the stack
activity.prompt: Place every protocol, device and PDU on its layer. Go fast the first time, then redo the ones you missed and say why each belongs there: "switch, Layer 2, because it reads MAC addresses".

check.question: Which OSI layer is responsible for logical addressing and choosing a path between networks?
check.explanation: Logical (IP) addressing and routing are Layer 3 jobs, which is why routers are called Layer 3 devices. Layer 2 delivers frames on one link using MAC addresses, and Layer 4 delivers data to the right application.

sections.title: The TCP/IP model and how it lines up with OSI
sections.key: TCP/IP's Application layer covers OSI Layers 5 to 7, Transport is 4, Internet (Network) is 3, and Link covers OSI Layers 1 and 2.
sections.body:
The protocols that run the internet come from the **TCP/IP model**. The original (RFC 1122) has four layers: Application, Transport, Internet and Link. Cisco's CCNA books draw five, splitting Link into Data Link and Physical. Expect both drawings; the mapping is what matters.

[[visual]]

Devices follow the same map:

[[visual 2]]

Why two models? OSI was a full protocol suite that lost the market, but its vocabulary stuck. You describe problems with OSI numbers and build networks with TCP/IP protocols.

visual.title: OSI layers, bracketed by TCP/IP layer
visual.caption: The five-layer CCNA drawing calls Internet **Network** and splits Link into **Data link** and **Physical**, matching OSI 1 to 4.

sections.pitfall: Putting switches at Layer 3 because they are smart. A standard switch reads MAC addresses only, so it is Layer 2. Only a Layer 3 (multilayer) switch also routes.

check.question: Which OSI layers does the TCP/IP Application layer cover?
check.explanation: TCP/IP folds Session, Presentation and Application (OSI 5 to 7) into one Application layer. Transport (Layer 4) remains its own layer in both models.

sections.title: Encapsulation and PDUs
sections.key: Each layer wraps the data in its header, making a segment, a packet, then a frame (the only PDU with a trailer); routers build a new frame at every hop.
sections.body:
A browser asks a web server for a page. On the way down the stack the request is wrapped once per layer: **encapsulation**. Each layer's unit is its **protocol data unit (PDU)**.

[[visual]]

[[visual 2]]

The receiver reverses it, **de-encapsulation**: check the FCS and strip the frame, strip the IP header, and hand the segment to TCP, which gives the data to the process on the destination port.

Between the hosts, every router de-encapsulates to Layer 3 and builds a **new frame** for the next link:

[[visual 3]]

visual.title: Encapsulation

layers.label: Segment
layers.detail: + TCP header: ports, sequence numbers (UDP: datagram)

layers.label: Packet
layers.detail: + IP header: source and destination IP, TTL, Protocol

layers.label: Frame
layers.detail: + Ethernet header: MACs, type; + FCS trailer

layers.label: Bits
layers.detail: signals on the wire or radio

visual.arrowLabel: Sending: each layer adds its header

visual.title: An Ethernet frame
visual.caption: The FCS trailer lets the receiver detect damaged frames.

visual.title: Across three routers, with no NAT
rows: **Yes**: every link gets a new frame
**Yes**: each router lowers it by 1, so a looping packet dies

sections.pitfall: Expecting the destination MAC to be the remote server. Off the local subnet, the destination MAC is always the next router (first the default gateway); only the IP points at the final host.

activity.title: Wrap, unwrap, rewrap
activity.prompt: Step through a packet crossing a router. At each hop, before advancing, predict which addresses will change. Check that the source and destination IP never change while the MAC addresses are replaced at every router.

check.question: What is the PDU called at the transport layer when TCP is used?
check.explanation: TCP's unit is the segment (Layer 4 PDU). IP builds packets at Layer 3, Ethernet builds frames at Layer 2, and the physical layer sends bits. UDP's unit is often called a datagram.

sections.title: Ports, sockets and multiplexing
sections.key: Port numbers pick the application: servers listen on well-known ports, clients use ephemeral source ports, and every reply swaps the two.
sections.body:
Your laptop has one IP address but runs six browser tabs, chat and mail at once. TCP and UDP headers carry a 16-bit source and destination **port** (0 to 65535), and delivering data to the right application with them is **multiplexing**, the one feature TCP and UDP share.

[[visual]]

A server **listens** on a well-known port. A client picks an unused ephemeral **source port** and sends to the server's **destination port**. The reply swaps them.

[[visual 2]]

A **socket** is an IP address, a transport protocol and a port: (192.168.1.20, TCP, 51514). A connection is a pair of sockets, so two tabs to one server stay apart by their source ports.

[[visual 3]]

visual.title: IANA port ranges
rows: Chosen by the client OS for its side (some OSes use other ranges)

visual.title: One laptop's TCP connections
visual.caption: `netstat -an` on Windows or `ss -tn` on Linux lists them.

sections.pitfall: Thinking ports identify computers. IP addresses identify hosts; ports identify applications (sockets) on those hosts.

check.question: A client at 10.1.1.10 uses source port 50123 to reach a web server on TCP port 80. What is the destination port in the server's reply?
check.explanation: Replies swap the ports: the server sends from its port 80 to the client's ephemeral port 50123, so the client's TCP knows which connection and application the data belongs to.

sections.title: Inside the headers: what TCP carries that UDP does not
sections.key: Every TCP feature has a header field (ports, sequence, acknowledgment, window, flags); UDP's 8-byte header keeps only ports, length and checksum.
sections.body:
You need not memorize layouts, but the fields explain every difference: if a feature needs a number, TCP has a field and UDP does not. The **TCP header** is 20 bytes without options (up to 60).

[[visual]]

[[visual 2]]

[[visual 3]]

Before reading Layer 4, a host knows what is inside from the IPv4 **Protocol** field (Next Header in IPv6): **6 is TCP, 17 is UDP**, 1 is ICMP. One layer down, the Ethernet type says IPv4 (0x0800) or IPv6 (0x86DD).

visual.title: Feature to field
rows: Flags: SYN, FIN (plus ACK, RST abort, PSH push now)

sections.tip: Map field to feature: ports = multiplexing, sequence and acknowledgment = reliability and ordering, window = flow control, SYN/FIN = connections.
sections.pitfall: Saying UDP has no error checking. UDP has a checksum and discards corrupted datagrams; what it lacks is error recovery, because nothing is acknowledged or resent.

check.question: Which TCP header field lets a receiver slow a fast sender down?
check.explanation: The window field advertises how many bytes the receiver will accept before the sender must wait for an acknowledgment. Sequence numbers handle ordering and gap detection, and the checksum only detects corruption.

sections.title: TCP connection setup and teardown
sections.key: TCP opens with SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK and closes each direction with FIN and ACK; a SYN answered by RST means the host is up but nothing listens.
sections.body:
TCP is **connection-oriented**: the two ends exchange messages before any data flows. A **connectionless** protocol such as UDP does not; its first datagram already carries data. TCP's agreement is the **three-way handshake**:

[[visual]]

Closing takes four segments, because each direction closes separately. **RST** (reset) aborts at once.

[[visual 2]]

The handshake doubles as a diagnostic:

[[visual 3]]

visual.title: Three-way handshake
visual.caption: Each side acknowledges the other's starting sequence number plus one.

visual.title: What answers a SYN?
rows: The host is reachable, but nothing listens on that port
A firewall or ACL dropped it, or the host is down

sections.deeper: Packet captures such as Wireshark usually show **relative** sequence numbers, starting each side at 0, so the handshake reads Seq=0, then Seq=0 Ack=1, then Seq=1 Ack=1. The real initial sequence numbers are random 32-bit values, chosen so that segments from an old connection cannot be mistaken for a new one.
sections.pitfall: Describing the handshake as four messages (SYN, ACK, SYN, ACK). The server combines its SYN and its ACK into one segment, which is why it is three-way.

activity.title: Handshake, loss and UDP
activity.prompt: Step through the handshake and write down the sequence and acknowledgment numbers at each step. Then drop a data segment and watch which acknowledgment number the receiver repeats. Finish by switching to UDP and notice what is missing.

check.question: What is the correct order of the TCP three-way handshake?
check.explanation: The client sends SYN, the server replies with one segment carrying both SYN and ACK, and the client finishes with ACK. Only then does application data flow.

sections.title: TCP reliability: sequence numbers, acknowledgments and retransmission
sections.key: TCP acknowledges the next byte it expects (forward acknowledgment); a gap makes the receiver repeat that number until the sending host retransmits the missing bytes.
sections.body:
TCP promises the application every byte, in order, without duplicates: **error recovery**. Each segment's **sequence number** names its first byte. The receiver's **acknowledgment number** names the **next byte it expects**: **forward acknowledgment**.

A browser sends three 1000-byte segments, sequence 1000, 2000 and 3000:

[[visual]]

With all three, the server would send ACK 4000 at once. A **retransmission timer** makes sure the sender does not wait forever for a missing acknowledgment. Sequence numbers also let the receiver reorder segments and discard duplicates.

This happens only in the two end hosts. Ethernet silently discards a frame that fails its FCS; switches and routers never resend. The data comes back because the sending host's TCP notices the missing acknowledgment: reliability is **end to end**.

visual.title: One segment lost
visual.caption: One acknowledgment covers both the resent segment and the one already stored.

sections.pitfall: Reading the acknowledgment number as the last byte received. It is always the next byte expected: the last byte received plus one.

check.question: A server receives segments with sequence numbers 1000 and 3000 (1000 bytes each), but the segment with sequence number 2000 is lost. What acknowledgment number does the server send?
check.explanation: Forward acknowledgment names the next byte expected. The server has everything up to 1999, so it asks for 2000. After the retransmission arrives it can acknowledge 4000 because it already holds 3000 to 3999.

sections.title: Flow control, windows and segmentation
sections.key: The receiver's advertised window caps how many unacknowledged bytes the sender may have in flight, and TCP cuts the byte stream into segments no larger than the MSS.
sections.body:
A fast server sends to a slow phone. Unchecked, the phone's buffer would overflow and the extra bytes would be lost and resent. **Flow control** prevents that with the **window**.

Every acknowledgment carries a window size: the bytes the sender may have sent but not yet acknowledged. With a window of 3000 and 1000-byte segments, the sender sends three, then waits.

[[visual]]

When all goes well the receiver grows the window, a **sliding** (dynamic) **window**. If its buffers fill, it shrinks it, even to **zero**, which pauses the sender until a larger window arrives.

TCP also does **segmentation**: it cuts the app's byte stream into segments no larger than the **maximum segment size (MSS)** agreed in the handshake.

[[visual 2]]

UDP does neither: each message is one datagram, sent at the application's pace.

messages.note: Window full: the sender must wait

steps.label: Start with the Ethernet payload (IP MTU)
Subtract the IP and TCP headers

sections.tip: The acknowledgment number answers what have you got; the window answers how much more can I send. Exam distractors swap the two.
sections.pitfall: Thinking routers use the TCP window to slow traffic. Flow control runs only between the two end hosts; routers forward segments without reading or changing the window.

check.question: A receiver advertises a window of 6000 bytes and the sender uses 1500-byte segments. How many segments can be outstanding before the sender must wait for an acknowledgment?
check.explanation: The window is a byte count: 6000 / 1500 = 4 segments may be unacknowledged at once. After that the sender waits for an ACK, which may also carry a new window size.

sections.title: UDP, and how to choose between TCP and UDP
sections.key: UDP is connectionless with an 8-byte header and no handshake, acknowledgments, ordering or windowing, which suits real-time media, tiny queries and broadcast or multicast.
sections.body:
A voice packet with 20 ms of speech goes missing. TCP would hold everything behind it until a resend arrived, too late: the call stutters. Better to skip it and go on. That is the job for **UDP** (User Datagram Protocol).

[[visual]]

UDP is not worse than TCP; it does less, and some applications want exactly that.

[[visual 2]]

When a UDP datagram reaches a port where nothing listens, there is no RST (UDP has no flags). The host answers with an **ICMP port unreachable** instead.

visual.title: TCP and UDP compared
rows: Web, email, SSH, file transfer, databases
Voice and video (RTP), DNS queries, DHCP, TFTP, SNMP, syslog, NTP

steps.label: Is it one small question and one small answer?
steps.yes: UDP: the app just retries (DNS, DHCP, SNMP, NTP, syslog, TFTP)

steps.label: Is it sent to a broadcast or multicast address?
steps.yes: UDP: TCP connects exactly two hosts (DHCP Discover)

steps.label: Every byte must arrive, in order

sections.deeper: TFTP runs over UDP but adds its own simple acknowledgments, one block at a time, so even a UDP application can be reliable if it builds that in. HTTP/3 goes further: it runs over **QUIC**, which uses UDP and rebuilds reliability, ordering and encryption inside the application. That is the real trade-off: UDP is a minimal transport that leaves the decisions to the app. A host with no IP address yet (a DHCP client) also cannot open a TCP connection at all, another reason DHCP uses UDP.
sections.pitfall: Saying UDP is unreliable, so never use it. For real-time media and tiny request-response exchanges its low overhead is exactly what you want.

check.question: Why do voice-over-IP media streams use UDP instead of TCP?
choices: Retransmitting a lost voice packet would arrive too late to be useful and would add delay
UDP guarantees in-order delivery for real-time traffic
check.explanation: Real-time audio cannot wait for a retransmission, so TCP's reliability would only add delay and jitter. UDP lets the application skip lost packets. UDP does not encrypt and does not guarantee ordering.

sections.title: Well-known ports the exam expects
sections.key: Know common ports with their transport: background management protocols (NTP, SNMP, syslog, TFTP) use UDP; protocols needing every byte (SSH, FTP, SMTP, HTTP) use TCP.
sections.body:
Firewall rules, ACLs and packet captures are full of port numbers, so recognize the common ones on sight, with TCP or UDP.

[[visual]]

Learn them as stories: FTP's TCP 20 and 21 versus TFTP's UDP 69; SSH (22, encrypted) replaced its neighbor Telnet (23, clear text); SMTP sends mail, POP3 and IMAP read it.

Always pair the port with the transport. An ACL permitting only `tcp ... eq 53` lets DNS zone transfers through but blocks ordinary lookups, which use UDP 53:

[[code]]

visual.title: Well-known ports
rows: DNS: UDP for queries, TCP for zone transfers and large replies

sections.code:
R1(config)# access-list 101 permit udp any host 10.9.9.53 eq 53
R1(config)# access-list 101 permit tcp any host 10.9.9.53 eq 53
sections.pitfall: Mixing up FTP and TFTP. FTP is TCP 20 and 21 with logins; TFTP is UDP 69 with no authentication, which is why devices use it for quick transfers on trusted networks.

check.question: Which application uses port 53 over both UDP and TCP?
check.explanation: DNS uses UDP 53 for most lookups and TCP 53 for zone transfers and replies too large for UDP. DHCP uses UDP 67 and 68, SNMP UDP 161 and 162, and TFTP UDP 69.

keyTerms.definition: Adding a layer's header (and for frames, a trailer) around the data from the layer above.
Protocol data unit: segment at Layer 4, packet at Layer 3, frame at Layer 2, bits at Layer 1.
An IP address, transport protocol and port number that identify one end of a conversation.
A temporary source port, usually 49152 to 65535, chosen by a client OS for one connection.
SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK: how TCP establishes a connection and synchronizes sequence numbers.
TCP acknowledges by naming the next byte it expects, not the last byte received.
TCP flow control: the receiver advertises how many bytes the sender may send before waiting for an ACK.
Sends data without any prior setup or shared state between the endpoints, as UDP does.
Ports 0 to 1023, reserved for standard server applications such as HTTPS on 443.
The name for a UDP message (header plus data). TCP calls its unit a segment.
The largest amount of data TCP puts in one segment, announced in the handshake. 1460 bytes on standard Ethernet.
TCP flag that aborts a connection immediately; a host sends it in reply to a SYN for a port where nothing listens.
A protocol that exchanges messages to set up a relationship before data flows, as TCP does with SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK.
IPv4 header field naming the payload: 6 for TCP, 17 for UDP, 1 for ICMP (Next Header in IPv6).

summary: OSI: Physical, Data Link, Network, Transport, Session, Presentation, Application; TCP/IP Application covers OSI 5 to 7.
Data, segment, packet, frame (the only PDU with a trailer), bits; routers build a new frame at every hop.
Servers listen on well-known ports, clients use ephemeral source ports, replies swap them.
TCP: handshake, forward acknowledgment, retransmission, windowing, MSS segmentation. UDP: 8 bytes, ports and checksum only.
UDP suits late-useless media, tiny queries and broadcast or multicast.
Know FTP 20/21, SSH 22, Telnet 23, SMTP 25, DNS 53, DHCP 67/68, TFTP 69, HTTP 80, POP3 110, NTP 123, IMAP 143, SNMP 161/162, HTTPS 443, syslog 514.
lesson.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a friend how their browser asks a website for a page: what gets wrapped around the request at each layer, how TCP makes sure nothing is lost, and why a video call would rather use UDP.

questions.question: Put the OSI layers in order from Layer 1 to Layer 7.
questions.explanation: From the bottom: Please Do Not Throw Sausage Pizza Away. Physical (1), Data Link (2), Network (3), Transport (4), Session (5), Presentation (6), Application (7).

questions.question: Routers forward packets by reading destination IP addresses. Which OSI layer is that?
questions.explanation: IP addressing and routing belong to the Network layer, Layer 3. Layer 2 uses MAC addresses within one link and Layer 4 uses port numbers.

questions.question: Following a bottom-up approach, a technician confirms the cable is good and the switch port shows up/up. Which should be checked next?
choices: The PC's IP address, mask and default gateway
Whether the web application is running
questions.explanation: Up/up confirms Layers 1 and 2. Bottom-up troubleshooting moves next to Layer 3: the IP address, mask and default gateway. Applications are Layer 7, the last step.

questions.question: The TCP software on a client writes a sequence number into its header, and the TCP software on the server reads it. Which concept does this describe?
questions.explanation: Same-layer interaction is a layer on one device communicating with the same layer on another device through its header. Adjacent-layer interaction is one layer providing a service to the layer above on the same device.

questions.question: Which OSI layers does the TCP/IP Link (network access) layer correspond to?
questions.explanation: The original TCP/IP Link layer covers both the physical signaling and the data link framing, OSI layers 1 and 2. The five-layer drawing in the Cisco books splits it back into Data Link and Physical.

questions.question: Match each item to the OSI layer where it belongs.

pairs.left: Data formats such as JPEG and ASCII

questions.explanation: Each device works at the layer whose information it reads: hubs only signals, switches MACs, routers IPs. Transport handles ports, presentation handles data formats, and application protocols sit on top.

questions.question: In the original TCP/IP model, which OSI layer does the Internet layer correspond to?
questions.explanation: The TCP/IP Internet layer is where IP lives, which is OSI Layer 3, Network. The five-layer drawing simply calls it Network.

questions.question: A host sends data to a remote server. Put the PDUs in the order they are created as the data moves down the stack.
questions.explanation: Application data is wrapped in a TCP header (segment), then an IP header (packet), then an Ethernet header and trailer (frame), and finally sent as bits.

questions.question: Which PDU includes a trailer as well as a header?
questions.explanation: The Ethernet frame has a header and a trailer, and the trailer holds the FCS used to detect bit errors. TCP segments, UDP datagrams and IP packets have headers only.

questions.question: PC1 sends a TCP segment to a server that is three router hops away, with no NAT anywhere. Which values are different in the frame that arrives at the server compared with the frame PC1 sent?
choices: The source and destination IP addresses
The source and destination MAC addresses and the IP TTL
The TCP source and destination ports
Nothing; the frame is forwarded unchanged
questions.explanation: Each router strips the incoming frame and builds a new one for the next link, so MAC addresses change at every hop, and each router decrements the TTL. IP addresses and ports stay the same end to end without NAT.

questions.question: Which two fields are carried in an Ethernet header? (Choose two.)
questions.explanation: The Ethernet header holds destination MAC, source MAC and the type field that says what is inside (IPv4 or IPv6). TTL and IP addresses are in the IP header, and ports are in the TCP or UDP header.

questions.question: Which range contains the well-known ports?
questions.explanation: Well-known (system) ports are 0 to 1023. 1024 to 49151 are registered ports, and 49152 to 65535 are dynamic (ephemeral) ports used by clients.

questions.question: A user opens two browser tabs to the same HTTPS server. How does the user's PC keep the two TCP connections apart?
choices: Each tab uses a different destination port on the server
Each tab uses a different IP address on the PC
TCP cannot run two connections to the same server
Each tab uses a different ephemeral source port
questions.explanation: Both connections go to the server's port 443, from the same client IP, but each uses its own ephemeral source port. The pair of sockets is unique, so replies reach the right tab.

questions.question: In the exhibit, which value was chosen dynamically by the PC's operating system for its SSH session?
questions.code:
C:\> netstat -an

Active Connections

  Proto  Local Address          Foreign Address        State
  TCP    0.0.0.0:445            0.0.0.0:0              LISTENING
  TCP    10.20.5.31:52210       198.51.100.69:443      ESTABLISHED
  TCP    10.20.5.31:52211       198.51.100.69:443      ESTABLISHED
  TCP    10.20.5.31:52230       192.0.2.25:22          ESTABLISHED
questions.explanation: The SSH session is the connection to port 22 on 192.0.2.25. Port 22 is the server's well-known port; the PC's side uses the ephemeral source port 52230. Port 445 is a local listening service and 443 belongs to the HTTPS connections.

questions.question: A client at 192.168.1.20 uses source port 61005 to open a connection to an SSH server at 10.1.1.5. What source port does the server use in its replies?
questions.explanation: The server answers from the port it listens on, the well-known SSH port 22, and sends to the client's ephemeral port 61005.

questions.question: Put the TCP three-way handshake in order.
questions.explanation: SYN opens the request and carries the client's initial sequence number, SYN-ACK acknowledges it and carries the server's number, and the final ACK completes the connection.

questions.question: A client sends a SYN with sequence number 7000. The server replies with SYN-ACK and its own sequence number 3000. What acknowledgment number does the server put in that SYN-ACK?
questions.explanation: The SYN consumes one sequence number, so the server acknowledges 7000 + 1 = 7001, meaning "the next byte I expect from you is 7001". The client's final ACK will carry acknowledgment number 3001.

questions.question: A client sends a TCP SYN to port 8080 on a server where no application is listening on that port. What does the server typically send back?
choices: A SYN-ACK, then it waits for data
A segment with the RST flag
Nothing, TCP never answers closed ports
questions.explanation: A host that receives a SYN for a port with no listener answers with RST (reset), refusing the connection. FIN is for closing an established connection gracefully.

questions.question: Which TCP flag tells the other side that the sender has finished sending data and wants to close its direction of the connection?
questions.explanation: FIN starts a graceful close for one direction. The other side ACKs it, sends its own FIN when it is done, and receives a final ACK, which is why the close takes four segments.

questions.question: A sender transmits three 1000-byte segments with sequence numbers 1000, 2000 and 3000. The segment with sequence 2000 is lost; the other two arrive. What acknowledgment number does the receiver send?
questions.explanation: TCP acknowledges the next byte it expects. The receiver has 1000 to 1999 but a gap starting at 2000, so it sends ACK 2000 even though it also holds 3000 to 3999. After the retransmission it can send ACK 4000.

questions.question: A receiver advertises a window of 4000 bytes. The sender uses 1000-byte segments. How many segments can it send before it must wait for an acknowledgment?
questions.explanation: The window is the number of unacknowledged bytes allowed in flight: 4000 / 1000 = 4 segments. Then the sender waits for an ACK that also tells it the new window.

questions.question: A web server sends a segment with acknowledgment number 4000 to a browser. What does that mean?
choices: The server received byte 4000 and nothing after it
The server wants the browser to resend everything from byte 0
The server received all bytes up to 3999 and expects byte 4000 next
The server can accept 4000 more bytes before acknowledging
questions.explanation: With forward acknowledgment, the number is the next byte expected, so everything through 3999 has arrived. How many bytes the browser may send before waiting is the window field, not the acknowledgment number.

questions.question: Which TCP mechanism lets a slow receiver tell a fast sender to send less data before waiting for an acknowledgment?
questions.explanation: The receiver advertises a window size in every ACK. Shrinking it slows the sender, and a window of zero pauses it. That is TCP flow control.

questions.question: Which three applications typically use UDP? (Choose three.)
questions.explanation: Real-time media, DHCP and TFTP use UDP. SSH, HTTP (before HTTP/3) and SMTP use TCP because they need every byte delivered in order.

questions.question: Which features does UDP provide?
choices: Port-based multiplexing and a checksum only
questions.explanation: UDP's 8-byte header has source port, destination port, length and checksum. It multiplexes by port and can detect corruption, but provides no handshake, ACKs, ordering or flow control.

questions.question: A developer builds a sensor app that sends a 60-byte temperature reading every second. A missing reading does not matter because the next one arrives a second later. Which transport fits and why?
choices: TCP, because every reading must be acknowledged
UDP, because the overhead of a connection and retransmissions buys nothing here
TCP, because UDP cannot carry small messages
UDP, because it guarantees the readings arrive in order
questions.explanation: When old data is useless and the next update replaces it, retransmission only adds overhead. UDP's small header and lack of connection setup fit. UDP does not guarantee ordering, and it handles small messages perfectly well.

questions.question: Match each port to its application.
questions.explanation: SSH 22 and Telnet 23 sit side by side; DHCP servers listen on UDP 67 and clients use 68; TFTP is UDP 69; HTTPS is TCP 443; SMTP is TCP 25.

questions.question: Match each application to its port.
questions.explanation: FTP uses 21 for control and 20 for data. Mail retrieval is POP3 110 (or IMAP 143). NTP, SNMP and syslog are UDP management protocols.

questions.question: Which TCP port does HTTPS use by default?
questions.explanation: HTTPS (HTTP over TLS) listens on TCP 443. Plain HTTP uses TCP 80.

questions.question: A firewall between a router and a file server permits only UDP port 69 from the router. Which transfer will work?
choices: Copying an IOS image with TFTP
questions.explanation: TFTP uses UDP 69. FTP needs TCP 20 and 21, and SCP and SSH need TCP 22, so they would all be blocked.

questions.question: A host receives an IPv4 packet. Before reading any Layer 4 header, how does it know the payload is a UDP datagram?
questions.explanation: The IPv4 Protocol field identifies the next header: 17 for UDP, 6 for TCP, 1 for ICMP. The Ethernet type field only says the frame carries IPv4, and port numbers live inside the UDP header itself.

questions.question: Which three fields are in the TCP header but not in the UDP header? (Choose three.)
questions.explanation: Sequence and acknowledgment numbers provide ordering and reliability, and the window provides flow control. UDP has none of them. Both headers carry source and destination ports and a checksum.

questions.question: How many bytes long is a UDP header?
questions.explanation: The UDP header has four 2-byte fields (source port, destination port, length, checksum), 8 bytes in total. A TCP header is at least 20 bytes.

questions.question: An engineer captures this traffic while a user reports that a web app on port 8080 "will not load". What does the capture show?
questions.code:
No. Source      Destination  Proto Info
1   10.1.1.10   10.2.2.20    TCP   50514 > 8080 [SYN] Seq=0
2   10.2.2.20   10.1.1.10    TCP   8080 > 50514 [RST, ACK] Seq=1 Ack=1
choices: A firewall between them is silently dropping the SYN
The server is reachable, but nothing is accepting connections on TCP 8080
The handshake completed and the server closed the connection after sending the page
The client should have used UDP for port 8080
questions.explanation: The server answered the SYN with RST, so it is reachable and its TCP stack is running, but no application is listening on port 8080 (or it refused the connection). A firewall dropping the SYN would produce silence and SYN retries, not an RST from the server.

questions.question: Host A has finished sending and closes a TCP connection gracefully. Put the four segments in order.
items: Host B sends its own FIN
questions.explanation: Each direction closes separately: A sends FIN, B acknowledges it, B sends its own FIN when it is done, and A acknowledges that. B may combine its ACK and FIN, but the logical order is the same.

questions.question: A receiver has every byte from 1 to 4000 in order, and also bytes 5001 to 6000. The segment holding bytes 4001 to 5000 was lost. What acknowledgment number does the receiver send?
questions.explanation: Forward acknowledgment names the next byte expected. Everything through 4000 arrived, so the receiver asks for 4001, even though it is already holding 5001 to 6000. Once 4001 to 5000 is resent, it can acknowledge 6001.

questions.question: A busy server advertises a TCP window of 0 to a client that is uploading a file. What does the client do?
choices: Sends a RST and opens a new connection
Keeps sending, because the window only applies to acknowledgments
Stops sending new data until the server advertises a larger window
questions.explanation: A zero window means "my buffer is full, send nothing more". The client pauses new data until the server advertises a nonzero window. It does not tear the connection down or switch transports.

questions.question: An application hands TCP 6000 bytes to send over Ethernet with an MSS of 1460. What is the minimum number of TCP segments needed?
questions.explanation: 6000 / 1460 is about 4.1, so four full segments (5840 bytes) are not enough and a fifth carries the last 160 bytes: 5 segments. Segmenting large data is a TCP job; UDP leaves message sizes to the application.

questions.question: Match each TCP feature to the header field or flags that make it work.
questions.explanation: Ports multiplex, sequence and acknowledgment numbers give reliability and ordering, the window gives flow control, SYN and FIN flags open and close connections, and the checksum detects corruption.

questions.question: A PC sends a UDP datagram to port 5000 on a server where no application is listening on that port. What typically comes back?
choices: A TCP segment with the RST flag
questions.explanation: UDP has no flags, so there is no RST. The receiving host typically returns an ICMP port unreachable message. TCP is the protocol that answers a closed port with RST.

questions.question: Which two requirements point an application designer toward UDP rather than TCP? (Choose two.)
choices: Sending one message to a multicast group
Every byte must arrive in order
Late data is useless, so low delay matters more than retransmission
Large files must be split and reassembled
questions.explanation: TCP connections are always between two hosts, so broadcast and multicast delivery need UDP, and real-time media prefers skipping late data over waiting for retransmissions. Guaranteed, in-order delivery and flow control are reasons to choose TCP.

questions.question: An ACL must let a branch router reach a DNS server for normal name lookups and for zone transfers. Which traffic must it permit to the server?
questions.explanation: DNS uses UDP 53 for ordinary queries and TCP 53 for zone transfers and replies too large for UDP. Permitting only one transport breaks half of DNS. Port 67 is DHCP.

questions.question: Which combination identifies a socket?
choices: IP address, transport protocol and port number
questions.explanation: A socket is an IP address, a transport protocol and a port number, for example 10.1.1.10, TCP, 51514. A connection is identified by the pair of sockets at its two ends.

questions.question: A switch receives a frame whose FCS check fails and discards it. The frame held part of a TCP file transfer. How is the missing data recovered?
choices: The switch asks the previous switch to resend the frame
The router at the next hop rebuilds the frame from its cache
The sending host retransmits after the receiver does not acknowledge those bytes
It is not recovered; TCP only detects errors
questions.explanation: Ethernet only detects errors; the switch drops the bad frame and does nothing more. The sending host notices the missing acknowledgment (or a repeated ACK for the same byte) and retransmits. Reliability lives in the end hosts.

questions.question: After this ACL is applied inbound on the branch LAN interface, users can no longer resolve names, although the DNS server at 10.9.9.53 is up. What is wrong?
questions.code:
R1# show access-lists 120
Extended IP access list 120
    10 permit tcp any host 10.9.9.53 eq domain (12 matches)
    20 permit tcp any host 10.9.9.25 eq smtp (310 matches)
    30 deny ip any any (1543 matches)
choices: Line 20 should use port 53 instead of smtp
DNS queries use UDP 53, and the ACL permits only TCP 53
The deny on line 30 should be moved to the top
The keyword domain means port 25 in IOS
questions.explanation: IOS shows well-known ports by name: domain is 53 and smtp is 25. Line 10 permits only TCP 53, but ordinary DNS queries use UDP 53, so they fall through to the deny on line 30. Adding a permit for udp to host 10.9.9.53 eq domain fixes it.
